name: GraphPlanner

paper.title: GraphPlanner: Graph Memory-Augmented Agentic Routing for Multi-Agent LLMs

construction.unit: interaction row: input node, (role, LLM) hub, output node, with task score and cost
construction.kept_as: Longformer embeddings of the step's input and output text; the text itself is not kept in memory
construction.processing: every routing step logs one row; no LLM processing of memory

organization.structure: heterogeneous graph: query and response nodes linked to one shared hub node per (role, LLM) pair
organization.stores: workflow memory (rows of the current query) and historical memory (rows of all training episodes)
organization.index: none; the whole graph is encoded by GARNet at every step

management.operations: append a finished training episode's workflow rows to the historical memory

retrieval.query: current node embedding fused with root-query and task-type embeddings
retrieval.candidates: all history rows, averaged per hub (no search or top-k)
retrieval.selection: policy score state · hub, masked to valid roles; sampled in training, argmax at test

use.context: memory only chooses the next (role, LLM); the LLM agents read text: original query, parent queries, sibling answers, summary
use.reasoning: multi-step planner / executor / summarizer workflow, 8.1 LLM calls per query on average in Phase 2

classify.note: Memory is read by a learned policy network, not searched: every history row is mean-pooled into its (role, LLM) hub at every decision. The output is an action (which role and LLM act next), not retrieved content.

stages.ingestion: Each step of a query's workflow (plan, answer or summarize, run by one LLM) produces a row: the embedding of the node being processed, the embedding of the LLM's output, the task score and the cost.
stages.construction: Rows are stored only as Longformer vectors plus two scalars; query and response nodes connect to a fixed hub node per (role, LLM) pair, whose feature is the role description embedding joined with the LLM description embedding.
stages.organization: Two graphs share the hubs: the workflow memory graph of the current query and the historical memory graph of past episodes; rounds are linked only through the shared hubs, not by temporal edges.
stages.update: During training the finished episode's rows are appended to the historical memory; nothing is merged or deleted. At test time the history is fixed and only the current query's rows grow.
stages.retrieval: At every step GARNet encodes the whole history (a scatter-mean per hub in the released code), injects the resulting hub vectors into the workflow graph encoder, and scores each hub against a fused state (node, root query, task type); invalid roles are masked.
stages.answer: The chosen LLM runs its role with a text prompt (original query, parent queries, sibling answers, summary); a final executor writes the answer. Memory vectors never enter a prompt.
stages.learning: The policy and value networks (GARNet) are trained with PPO on task score; the paper's reward also subtracts alpha times cost, the released code rewards only the final score.

summary: An RL-trained router that decides, step by step, which agent role and which LLM act next, reading a heterogeneous graph memory of past and current (query, role-LLM, response) interactions.
notes:
Venue: ICLR 2026 main conference, verified on the PDF header ('Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026') and the arXiv journal reference. Scope: memory here is interaction history for routing decisions, not user or task content; nothing from memory reaches an LLM prompt.
CODE: released dynamic_router at commit 56010b1 (2026-04-26) read in full for the memory path; static_router is the Phase-1 fixed-workflow variant and was not traced. Paper and code differ on the LLM pool (5 vs 10), the reward (no cost term in code) and PPO settings; see mechanism.paper_vs_code.

sources.code_note: Commit 56010b1 (2026-04-26) is the head of the repository and was pushed the same day as arXiv v1; the history has three commits, all on that day, so this is the only released version. The Phase-2 (dynamic) router is traced; the Phase-1 static router shares the design.

headline: Memory stores no text: each step is two Longformer vectors plus a score and a cost, attached to a (role, LLM) hub.
History is not searched. Every row is averaged into its hub at every step, so the history signal for an action is the same for every query.
The graph only decides who acts next; the LLM agents themselves read plain-text context (parent queries, sibling answers, summary).

after a training episode, all its workflow rows are appended to the historical memory; no dedup, merge or deletion
write.note: not done at test time: test episodes read the training history but never add to it

read.scores: no matching; every row joins its hub
read.how: per-table linear layer, then scatter-mean of rows onto their hub id, added back to the hub (one DBLayer)
read.src: paper §3.2 'nested dual-graph encoding'; code network.py L58-L172, L253-L262

read.how: same layer over the current workflow rows, starting from the history-enriched hubs

read.input: fused state: current node, root query, task type
read.scores: dot product with every hub vector
read.how: mask invalid roles, softmax; sample in training, argmax at test

params.actions: 3 roles x LLMs (15 in code, 30 in paper)

answer_context.sees: text only: the task query, the query hierarchy, earlier sibling answers and the root summary
answer_context.format: 'Full context' + 'Summary of sub-query responses' + the task-formatted query (final executor prompt)

compression.what: stored row vs the step's text
compression.basis: Not reported. Each side of a step is stored as one 768-d Longformer vector (texts up to 4096 tokens).

paper_vs_code.code: the dynamic router keeps 5 of 14 configured LLMs (qwen2.5-7b, codegemma-7b, gemma-2-9b, llama3-chatqa-1.5-8b, mistral-7b), 15 actions

paper_vs_code.paper: final utility minus alpha x cost at every step (Eq. 4)
paper_vs_code.code: final task score only; cost is stored as a feature, never subtracted
gamma 0.98, 1 epoch, lr 1e-4 (RouteAgent defaults, not overridden)

paper_vs_code.paper: role-LLM text embedding joined with utility and cost
paper_vs_code.code: role and LLM description embeddings only; score and cost sit on the rows

paper_vs_code.paper: Table 8: e.g. HumanEval 120 train / 44 test, GPQA 400 / 44, MATH 500 / 50
paper_vs_code.code: released CSVs: HumanEval 164 / 50, GPQA 448 / 50, MATH 504 / 56; 11 tasks, no out-of-domain tasks

open_questions: Does the history help because it describes past interactions, or because it gives each hub a learned per-action prior? In the code each hub gets one mean over all its rows, the same for every query, and no ablation separates the two.
The w/o History, Homo-Graph and Hetero-Graph ablation (Fig. 5b) and the inductive vs transductive comparison (Fig. 5c) are shown only as radar plots, without numbers.

text: Each step of a query's workflow (plan, answer or summarize, done by one LLM) is logged as a row: the input and output as Longformer vectors, tied to that role-and-LLM hub with its score and cost.
Rows of the current query form the workflow memory; after each training episode they are appended to the historical memory, which is never pruned.

text: At every step the policy averages all history rows into their hubs, adds the current query's rows, and scores each hub against the current state.
The best valid (role, LLM) runs next and adds a new row. The LLMs themselves read only text context, never the memory.

discussion.takeaway: Routing across LLMs can be framed as building a multi-agent workflow, with a small RL policy reading a graph of past and current (query, role-LLM, response) interactions. In its own tests this beats single- and multi-round routers on accuracy with far less training compute.

claims.evidence: Phase 2 average 63.6 vs 54.3 (RouterDC) and 51.8 (Router-R1); Phase 1 58.60 vs 54.80 (d1w3) and 60.40 vs 56.20 (d2w2). Tables 2-3
1.04 GiB GPU memory vs 186.26 GiB for Router-R1; 120 min total training vs 300. Tables 4, 15

claims.claim: Generalizes to unseen tasks and LLMs.
claims.evidence: LogicGrid / MGSM / CommonGen average 78 vs 58 (RouterDC); AIME 14.7 vs 7.56. Tables 5, 14; unseen LLMs only in Fig. 5a

claims.claim: Historical memory is essential, and GARNet uses it better than generic GNNs or LLM-read history.
claims.evidence: Fig. 5b (radar, w/o History drops most); Table 12 (GAT, GraphTransformer lower); Table 13 (Router-R1 with retrieved or summarized history 0.12-0.62 vs 0.38-0.78)

claims.claim: Transductive inference (keep training history) is slightly better than inductive but costlier.

limits: Only three agent roles (planner, executor, summarizer); richer roles are left to future work.
reading: Memory holds no user or task content: it is a log of routing outcomes stored as vectors, and nothing from it reaches an LLM prompt.

In the released code the history is not matched to the query: each hub receives the mean of all its rows, identical for every question, so its effect is closer to a learned per-action prior than to retrieval.

Costs are not comparable across the result tables: GraphPlanner averages 605.0 cost units and 8.1 calls per query in Phase 2, against 76.3 and 1.8 for Router-R1; the Pareto claim rests on Fig. 4 only.
The printed Average column is not the mean of the five domain columns (GraphPlanner 63.6 vs 62.2 by hand; Router-R1 51.8 vs 48.9), so it is presumably weighted by test items; the paper does not say.
Test sets are small (44-50 questions per task, Table 8), and one percentage point on a domain is about one question.
Released code differs from the paper in the LLM pool (5 vs 10), the reward (no cost term) and PPO settings, so the code as released does not reproduce the reported configuration.
The three memory ablations are radar plots without numbers; the only numeric memory ablation (Table 13) compares against Router-R1 variants, not GraphPlanner without history.

abstract.text: GraphPlanner treats LLM routing as building a small multi-agent workflow per query: at each step it chooses both an agent role (planner, executor or summarizer) and which LLM plays it. The choice is made by a graph neural policy, GARNet, that reads a heterogeneous graph of the current workflow and of past interactions, linking queries and responses to shared role-LLM nodes. The whole router is trained with PPO for accuracy and cost. Across 14 tasks the authors report higher accuracy than single- and multi-round routers, far lower training GPU memory, and zero-shot transfer to unseen tasks and LLMs.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.
